CHAPTER IX

FOES OR FRIENDS (1862)

Of the year 1862 Henry Adams could never think without a shudder. The war alone did not greatly distress him; already in his short life he was used to seeing people wade in blood, and he could plainly discern in history that man from the beginning had found his chief amusement in bloodshed; but the ferocious joy of destruction at its best requires that one should kill what one hates, and young Adams neither hated nor wanted to kill his friends the rebels, while he wanted nothing so much as to wipe England off the earth. Never could any good come from that besotted race! Every day the British Government deliberately crowded him one step further into the grave. The Trent Affair showed where Palmerston and Russell stood. The escape of the rebel cruisers from Liverpool was not, in a young man's eyes, the sign of hesitation, but the proof of their fixed intention to intervene. Lord Russell's replies to Mr. Adams's notes were discourteous in their indifference, and, to an irritable young private secretary of twenty-four, insolent in their disregard of truth. Not for an instant did the Legation draw a free breath. The suspense was hideous and unendurable.

He bore it as well as he could till midsummer; but when the story of the second Bull Run appeared, he could bear it no longer, and after a sleepless night, walking up and down his room without reflecting that his father was beneath him, he announced at breakfast his intention to go home into the army. His parents received it quietly; in those days, parents got used to all sorts of announcements from their children. He found obstacles constantly rising in his path. His brother Charles, already in the Army of the Potomac, remonstrated; he felt, too, that if he deserted his post in London and found only bullets to wound him in Virginia, he would never forgive himself for leaving his father and mother alone to be devoured by the wild beasts of the British amphitheatre. His father's suggestion was decisive: it was too late for the actual campaign; long before next spring they would all go home together. The young man had copied too many affidavits about rebel cruisers to miss the point. He sat down again to copy some more.

Not the work, but the play exhausted. The effort of facing a hostile society was bad enough; that of facing friends was worse. After terrific disasters like the seven days before Richmond and the second Bull Run, friends needed support; nothing answered but candor; yet private secretaries never feel candid, however much they feel the reverse, and therefore they must affect candor; not always a simple act when one is exasperated, furious, bitter, and choking with tears over the blunders and incapacity of one's Government. One must read one's Times every morning over one's muffin without reading aloud—“Another disastrous Federal Defeat”; and one might not even indulge in harmless profanity. One day, in the throne-room while the endless procession made bows to the royal family, he heard behind his shoulder one Cabinet Minister remark gaily to another: “So the Federals have got another licking!” Even a private secretary had learned to control his tones, guard his features, and betray no joy over the “lickings” of an enemy—in the enemy's presence.

London created a nightmare of its own and gave it the shape of Abraham Lincoln; behind it, if possible more devilish, it placed Mr. Seward. Defence was useless; explanation was vain. The last time Henry Adams saw Thackeray, before his sudden death that Christmas, was at an evening reception. Thackeray, laughing at having stumbled into the wrong house, changed tone as he spoke of his—and Adams's—friend, Mrs. Frank Hampton of South Carolina, whom he had loved as Sally Baxter and painted as Ethel Newcome. Hearing that she had died at Columbia while her parents and sister were refused permission to pass the lines to see her, his voice trembled and his eyes filled with tears. The coarse cruelty of Lincoln and his hirelings was notorious. On quite insufficient evidence he burst into violent reproach. Had Adams carried in his pocket the proofs that the reproach was unjust, he would have gained nothing by showing them. At that moment London needed the relief of expressing emotion; for if Mr. Lincoln was not what they said he was—what were they?

For like reason, the members of the Legation kept silence, even in private, under the boorish Scotch jibes of Carlyle. If Carlyle was wrong, his diatribes would give his true measure, and this measure would be a low one; the demolition of one's idols is painful, and Carlyle had been an idol. Not merely the idols fell, but also the habit of faith.

Society as a rule was civil, and one had no more reason to complain than every other diplomatist has had, in like conditions; the best they could do was to escape mortification. Diplomacy served as a buffer. Henry Adams went his way peacefully enough, seeing clearly that society cared little to make his acquaintance, and seeing also no reason why it should discover charms in him of which he was himself unconscious. For a thousand reasons, the best diplomatic house in London was Lord Palmerston's, while Lord John Russell's was one of the worst. Lady Palmerston's evenings—Saturday Reviews, they were called—had great vogue; Cambridge House, without being young or smart, succeeded because she was “sympathique.” The small fry of the Legations were tolerated, pleased to stand in a corner and look at a bishop or even a duke. This was the social diversion of young Adams. The last Saturday evening he ever attended, his name was shouted up the staircase by gradations—“Mr. Handrew Hadams!”—“Mr. Hanthony Hadams!”—till he was finally announced as “Mr. Halexander Hadams,” and under this name made his bow for the last time to Lord Palmerston.

Far down the staircase one heard Lord Palmerston's laugh as he stood at the door receiving his guests. The laugh was singular, mechanical, wooden—“Ha! ... Ha! ... Ha!”—each a slow, deliberate ejaculation, as though he meant to say: “Yes! ... Yes! ... Yes!” by way of assurance; a laugh of 1810 and the Congress of Vienna. Palmerston loved foreign affairs and could no more resist scoring a point in diplomacy than in whist. Diplomats warned new colleagues that they might expect to be sacrificed by him to any momentary personal object; the Queen herself had complained. The worst liars were the candid; what one wanted to know was the motive that lay beyond the expression. Palmerston laid traps; Lady Palmerston tried to help victims; and her house became the only political house that worked.

Ministers of foreign powers, to hold him at arm's-length, were obliged to court the actual Foreign Secretary, Lord John Russell, who in 1861 was called up to the House of Lords. By some process of personal affiliation, Minister Adams persuaded himself that he could trust Russell more safely than Palmerston. His son, being young and ill-balanced, thought there was nothing to choose. With both, the months of education began to count as æons.

At last the rush came, as unexpected as always. Late one afternoon in June, 1862, as the private secretary returned with the Minister, he saw his father pick up a note and read it in silence; then he said curtly: “Palmerston wants a quarrel!” The matter was General Butler's woman-order at New Orleans, but the motive was the belief in Lincoln's brutality that had taken such root. Knowing Palmerston's habits, the Minister took for granted that he meant to produce this note in the House of Commons. If he did this at once, the Minister was lost; the quarrel was made. What followed belongs to history. As education, it had a value apart. Mr. Adams succeeded in muzzling Palmerston without a public scandal, and then, by a step excessively strong, closed private relations as well as public—refusing to receive further communications from him except through Lord Russell. It cost even the private secretary his invitations to Cambridge House. Lady Palmerston tried her best, but the two ladies found no resource except tears. Palmerston submitted and kept silence. Incredible as it seemed, he behaved like a well-bred gentleman who felt himself in the wrong. Perhaps Russell interposed; perhaps not. Palmerston had wanted a quarrel; when the quarrel was made, he backed out of it. Whether more angry with Butler, or more annoyed at himself for an unpardonable bêtise, the private secretary could never decide. The puzzle was part of his education in politics.

The tide of English feeling ran so violently against the Legation that one could only wait to see whether McClellan would bring relief. The year 1862 was a dark spot in Henry Adams's life, and the education it gave he gladly forgot. Towards its close he was flattered by an invitation from Monckton Milnes to Fryston—one of his many acts of charity to the young. A dispirited private secretary was exceedingly grateful; chiefly as education the visit had value. Milnes mixed strange elements to astonish each other. Of the guests, one alone concerned Adams's education.

In due course the five sat down to dinner; conversation drifted till Milnes brought out Mr. Algernon Swinburne. Then, at last, if never before, Adams acquired education. For the rest of the evening Swinburne figured alone. Smoking being forbidden, Milnes licensed his guests to smoke in Adams's room, and there all sat—or lay—till far into the night, listening to the rush of Swinburne's talk. No one ever approached it. They could not believe his incredible memory and knowledge of literature, classic, mediæval, and modern; his faculty of reciting a play of Sophocles or of Shakespeare, forward or backward; his rhetorical declamation of his own unpublished ballads—“Faustine,” the “Four Boards of the Coffin Lid,” the “Ballad of Burdens”—as though they were books of the Iliad. His humor united them even more than his poetry. Late at night, when the symposium broke up, a Scotchman, at the climax of his wonder, burst out: “He's a cross between the devil and the Duke of Argyll!”

Then came the Boston reaction; not from Swinburne, whose genius was not in doubt, but from the Boston mind which was never moyenâgeux. What could a shy young private secretary do? The attitude of prayer is possible only in France; in England it becomes absurd. Swinburne tested him there and then by one of his favorite tests—Victor Hugo. French verse requires extraordinary knowledge of the language and rare refinement of ear. Adams had neither. He tried to evade the test by parading an affection for Alfred de Musset. Swinburne would have none of it; de Musset was unequal; he did not sustain himself on the wing. Swinburne tried him again on Walter Savage Landor, whom he admired for the qualities he felt in Hugo. Driven to despair, Adams had to admit that both Hugo and Landor bored him. Nothing more was needed. One who could feel neither Hugo nor Landor was lost.

The sentence was just, and Adams never appealed. Keenly mortified by the dullness of his senses and instincts, he knew he could be only an annoyance; no number of centuries could ever educate him to Swinburne's level, even in technical appreciation. He often wondered whether there was nothing he had to offer worth acceptance. Even Milnes, who felt the splendors of Hugo and Landor, was almost as helpless as an American secretary in personal contact. Years later, bubbling with delight at a call he had made on Hugo, he told how he was shown into a large room with women and men seated against the walls, and Hugo at one end throned. No one spoke. At last Hugo raised his voice solemnly, and uttered: “Quant à moi, je crois en Dieu!” Silence followed. Then a woman responded as if in deep meditation: “Chose sublime! un Dieu qui croit en Dieu!”

As soon as he reached town Adams hurried to buy “Queen Rosamund.” When the “Poems and Ballads” came out and met their success and scandal, he sought one of the first copies; if he had sinned and doubted at all, he wholly repented and did penance before “Atalanta in Calydon,” and would have offered Swinburne a solemn worship, if it would have pleased the poet. Unfortunately it was worthless.

The three young men returned to London, and each went his own way. “The London season,” Milnes used to say, “is a season for making acquaintances and losing friends.” Of Swinburne he saw no more till Milnes summoned his Frystonians to support him at the Authors' Fund dinner; Adams found himself seated next to Swinburne—famous then—but no nearer. They never met again. Others too disappeared. Immediately afterwards Milnes proposed Henry Adams for membership of the St. James's Club; the nomination was endorsed by kind hands; and on the whole it suggested that the private secretary was getting on.
